events.title: The millennium rollover causes limited disruption
events.description: The GAO reports limited disruptions following extensive preparation, while documenting some errors and their resolution.

events.title: The Nasdaq reaches its technology-boom peak
events.description: The Nasdaq Composite reaches a closing peak on March 10. Its later decline makes this a turning point in retrospect, not a signal available at the starting date.

events.title: September 11 attacks disrupt the United States
events.description: Attacks in New York and Washington are followed by a four-day equity trading halt. Markets reopen on September 17 amid central-bank responses.

events.title: The NBER announces a recession
events.description: The committee identifies March 2001 as the end of the long expansion. Business-cycle dating is retrospective; the turning point was not officially known in March.

events.title: The Fed begins raising its policy target
events.description: The Federal Reserve raises its federal funds target from 1% to 1.25%, describing solid economic expansion.

what_happened_next.text:
Technology companies and the internet kept attracting attention after September 1999. The Nasdaq, which tracks share prices for many technology companies, peaked in March 2000. It then fell for several years, with some sharp rises along the way.

The U.S. economy went from growing to shrinking. A group that tracks the economy later marked March 2001 as the recession’s start and November 2001 as its end. The September 11 attacks brought terrible loss of life and disrupted markets while the economy was already weakening. By June 2004, the economy was growing again and the Federal Reserve had started raising interest rates.

The results differed. A mix of many U.S. stocks and international stocks ended near where they started. Cash grew a little, and U.S. government bonds, a kind of loan, grew more. Microsoft, Cisco, and Amazon each ended below their September 1999 starting value, though their paths were different.

The year 2000 passed with fewer computer problems than many had feared, after years of preparation. People in September 1999 could not know how these five years would unfold.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: People followed software rivalries, new internet businesses, the coming year 2000, troubles in other countries, storms, sports, and entertainment.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The stock market fell, and the economy moved into and then out of a recession. Choosing one company instead of a basket of many companies could lead to very different results.
reflection.what_faded_away: Many people worried that computers would fail when calendars changed to 2000. After years of preparation, the new year came with little disruption. Product stories and sports soon made way for other news.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: In September 1999, no one knew when technology stocks would fall, how long the slide would last, or when the economy would go into recession. No one could know the September 11 attacks were coming. Popular companies did not make the future certain.
